analysis.one_liner: Caps child care costs at 7% of income for working families and raises provider pay.
analysis.headline: Backed by 33 senators — 32 Democrats and 1 independent — the bill was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup, a hearing vote, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap what low- and moderate-income families pay for child care at 7% of their income, with no copayment at all for families below 75% of their state's median income. It would expand eligibility for child care assistance from 85% to 150% of state median income, direct $20 billion in 2018 rising to $40 billion in 2020 to states, and require states to pay child care staff wages comparable to elementary school teachers with similar credentials, at no less than a living wage. A second title would fund voluntary high-quality preschool for 3-to-5-year-olds through state formula grants.
analysis.who_benefits: Working families with young children, especially those earning from 75% to 150% of their state's median income, who today often pay a fifth or more of their pay in child care costs. Child care teachers and aides benefit directly: the bill requires states to pay them wages comparable to elementary educators with similar credentials, at minimum a living wage, and to base reimbursement rates on the actual cost of delivering care. Children with disabilities, homeless children, and children in foster care receive priority slots and inclusive-care requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working families and child care workers

how_it_helps.text: Caps what no low- to moderate-income family pays for child care at 7% of household income.
Sets a sliding copayment scale: families below 75% of state median income pay nothing, and copayments top out at 2%, 4%, or 7% of income as income rises to 150% of state median income.
Expands the income ceiling for child care assistance from 85% to 150% of state median income, phased in over three years.

Requires state payment rates to cover the real cost of care at each quality tier and to pay child care staff wages comparable to elementary educators with similar credentials, and at minimum a living wage.
Authorizes $20 billion for fiscal 2018, $30 billion for 2019, and $40 billion for 2020 for child care assistance, plus necessary sums thereafter.

Creates Title II formula grants so states can offer voluntary high-quality preschool to all 3-to-5-year-olds from families up to 150% of state median income, with staff paid on the same scale as elementary educators.

Directs priority access and inclusive-care support to children with disabilities, homeless children, and children in foster care, and bars providers receiving assistance from suspending or expelling children.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the $20 billion to $40 billion per year in appropriations, which the bill writes as mandatory spending with no specified offset in its text. State taxpayers would cover the share of child care expenditures not covered by the federal matching formula, and states would face significant new planning duties: building cost-estimation models, tiered quality-rating systems, and wage ladders within three years.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $20 billion, $30 billion, and $40 billion for fiscal years 2018 through 2020 and 'such sums as may be necessary' every year after, written as appropriations without a stated funding source — a major addition to mandatory federal spending that an honest supporter would have to figure out how to pay for.

It imposes substantial new federal requirements on states — cost-estimation models, tiered quality systems, wage ladders, and consumer-reporting duties — and only pays 50% of state administrative costs, leaving states to absorb planning and compliance burdens in the early transition years.

Expanding eligibility to 150% of state median income and guaranteeing rates that cover provider costs would sharply increase demand for scarce slots; until supply catches up, families could face harder-to-find openings even as their bills shrink, and small informal providers could face pressure to meet new quality tiers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete: a hard 7%-of-income cap would transform the finances of most families with young children, and the wage provisions attack the root cause of quality problems — poverty pay for child care workers — rather than just subsidizing demand. The cost is equally large and honestly presented: $40 billion a year in open-ended federal spending with no offset specified, plus real transition burdens on states. This is one of the biggest social-policy expansions ever written into a bill, and its main weakness is that it never settles how it would be financed.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Senate health committee the same day it was introduced and stayed there; the committee never acted on it, and the Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced S. 1806 in the Senate on September 14, 2017, with 27 original cosponsors including the Democratic leadership's Sen. Schumer.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions that same day.
It drew 33 cosponsors in total — 32 Democrats and 1 independent, and no Republicans.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever recorded; the bill sat in committee until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
A nearly identical companion bill in the House (H.R. 2401, Rep. Katherine Clark) also died without a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No family with young children is better off — child care costs kept rising for them. The parties better served by the outcome are the federal budget (taxpayers never took on the $20-40 billion annual commitment) and existing child care providers, who continue operating under the current system with no new wage floors or quality obligations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal budget and incumbent providers

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.role: U.S. Senator (WA), bill sponsor; minority member of the HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Wrote and introduced the bill with 27 original cosponsors on September 14, 2017.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chairman, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup after it was referred; the committee took no recorded action on it during the entire 115th Congress.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; no floor action of any kind appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and not a single Republican signed on; the committee that never acted on it was chaired by a Republican, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled Senate.

industries.industry: Child care providers (centers, family child care homes, informal caregivers)
industries.note: The bill routes its new funding through these providers, paying them rates set to cover their true costs and raising staff wages to educator-comparable levels — a major revenue and payroll gain that arrives because families get relief. It also cements the mixed public-private system in which taxpayer child care dollars permanently flow through private providers rather than creating a public option.

industries.industry: Head Start and public school preschool programs
industries.note: Head Start grantees and local school districts are named eligible providers for the new preschool grants, and preschool programs must coordinate with Head Start and IDEA services. The expansion of preschool runs through them.

States receive a large infusion of federal money and a 50% federal match on administrative costs, but take on new duties — cost-estimation models, quality-tier systems, and wage ladders — that they must build largely at their own expense in early years.
